claim: Stem cells have characteristic properties including the ability to self-renew and to differentiate.
source: The characteristic properties of stem cells – notably their ability to self-renew and to differentiate – have meant that they have traditionally been viewed as distinct from most other types of cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about stem cell properties in the abstract.

claim: Recent research has shown that stem cells display a range of behaviors in different tissues and at different stages of development.
source: However, recent research has blurred the line between stem cells and other cells by showing that the former display a range of behaviors in different tissues and at different stages of development.
evidence: This is presented as a general finding from recent research without specific citations in this sentence.

claim: Stem cells have been traditionally described as a discrete population of cells sitting at the apex of a hierarchy of irreversible cell differentiation.
source: Stem cells have been described as a discrete population of cells sitting at the apex of a hierarchy of irreversible cell differentiation.
evidence: This describes the traditional view of stem cells as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The traditional view of stem cells has encouraged the idea that specific markers may help to distinguish and sort stem cells.
source: This view has had an impact on the way in which stem cell research is performed by, for example, encouraging the idea that specific markers may help to distinguish and sort stem cells.
evidence: This is an inference about how the traditional view influenced research approaches.

claim: Intestinal cells can replace the stem cells tasked with renewing the lining of the bowel.
source: For example, it appeared that intestinal cells could replace the stem cells tasked with renewing the lining of the bowel (Tetteh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tetteh et al., 2016.

claim: The flexibility of intestinal cells to replace stem cells suggests that stemness might not be restricted to a pre-defined population of cells.
source: Such flexibility suggested that stemness might not be restricted to a pre-defined population of cells and prompted some biologists to question what stem cells really were.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation about intestinal cell flexibility.

claim: Traditional views of stem cells arose from studies of the hematopoietic tissue in the bone marrow.
source: Traditional views of stem cells arose from studies of the hematopoietic tissue in the bone marrow, where blood cells originate in adults.
evidence: This is presented as historical knowledge about the origin of stem cell concepts.

claim: Blood cells originate in the bone marrow in adults.
source: Traditional views of stem cells arose from studies of the hematopoietic tissue in the bone marrow, where blood cells originate in adults.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge about hematopoiesis.

claim: Ray Schofield suggested in the late 1970s that stemness relies on the interaction of hematopoietic stem cells with their microenvironment.
source: However, in the late 1970s, Ray Schofield suggested that stemness actually relies on the interaction of hematopoietic stem cells (the cells that give rise to other blood cells) with the microenvironment in which they reside (Schofield, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schofield, 1978.

claim: Hematopoietic stem cells are the cells that give rise to other blood cells.
source: However, in the late 1970s, Ray Schofield suggested that stemness actually relies on the interaction of hematopoietic stem cells (the cells that give rise to other blood cells) with the microenvironment in which they reside (Schofield, 1978).
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established biological knowledge.

claim: The importance of the stem cell niche was long denied but is now increasingly accepted.
source: Although long denied, the importance of this 'niche' is now increasingly accepted: hematopoietic stem cells cannot be understood out of their context, which may account for the difficulties in maintaining them in culture.
evidence: This describes a historical shift in scientific understanding.

claim: Hematopoietic stem cells cannot be understood out of their context.
source: Although long denied, the importance of this 'niche' is now increasingly accepted: hematopoietic stem cells cannot be understood out of their context, which may account for the difficulties in maintaining them in culture.
evidence: This is an inference based on the importance of the niche.

claim: The importance of the niche may account for the difficulties in maintaining hematopoietic stem cells in culture.
source: Although long denied, the importance of this 'niche' is now increasingly accepted: hematopoietic stem cells cannot be understood out of their context, which may account for the difficulties in maintaining them in culture.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about why culture is difficult.

claim: Not every individual hematopoietic stem cell appears to be multipotent.
source: Finally, new technologies, such as lineage tracing, have further questioned the boundaries of the stem cell category, as studies have shown that not every individual hematopoietic stem cell appears to be multipotent (discussed in Haas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Haas et al., 2018.

claim: Non-hematopoietic stem cells called multipotent progenitors can maintain the production of hematopoietic cells over an extended period of time.
source: These analyses highlighted that non-hematopoietic stem cells, called multipotent progenitors, could unexpectedly maintain the production of hematopoietic cells over an extended period of time (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2014.

claim: There are two opposite views of what a stem cell is: it can be an entity (a discrete population of cells with stable properties) or a cell state (a property acquired in a specific context).
source: These are only a few of the examples that illustrate the potential diversity of these cells, which has resulted in two opposite views of what a stem cell is: it can either be an entity, a discrete population of cells with stable properties, or it can be a cell state, a property that is acquired in a specific context (e.g. Clevers and Watt, 2018; Zipori, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clevers and Watt, 2018 and Zipori, 2004.

claim: Four types of properties may exist under the guise of stemness.
source: We recently used this tradition to characterize stemness and our analysis led us to the conclusion that four types of properties may exist under the guise of stemness (Laplane, 2016; Laplane and Solary, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' own previous work.

claim: Stemness can be a categorical property, which is an intrinsic feature independent of any interaction with surrounding entities.
source: Stemness can be a 'categorical' property, that is, an intrinsic feature that is independent of any interaction with surrounding entities, such as the atomic mass of an element.
evidence: This is a definitional claim based on metaphysical analysis.

claim: It was initially assumed that all stem cells belong to the categorical property class.
source: It was initially assumed that all stem cells belong to this class, but, as discussed below, it might only apply to certain cancers.
evidence: This describes a historical assumption in the field.

claim: Categorical stemness might only apply to certain cancers.
source: It was initially assumed that all stem cells belong to this class, but, as discussed below, it might only apply to certain cancers.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Stemness can be a dispositional property, which is an intrinsic feature that only manifests upon interaction with external stimuli.
source: Alternatively, stemness can be a 'dispositional' property, which is also an intrinsic feature, but one that only manifests upon interaction with external stimuli.
evidence: This is a definitional claim based on metaphysical analysis.

claim: Healthy hematopoietic stem cells have stemness as a dispositional property.
source: Current knowledge suggests that healthy hematopoietic stem cells fall under this category.
evidence: This is an inference based on current scientific knowledge.

claim: Stemness in healthy hematopoietic stem cells is hardwired but tightly depends on the bone marrow niche.
source: Although stemness is hardwired in these cells, it tightly depends on the bone marrow niche.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dispositional property characterization.

claim: Hematopoietic progenitor cells can gain stemness as they transform into malignant cells.
source: In a malignant context, however, hematopoietic progenitor cells can gain stemness as they transform into malignant cells, questioning the maintenance of stemness as a dispositional property.
evidence: This is presented as an observation that questions the dispositional property model.

claim: Stemness can be a relational property that relies on the interaction between entities.
source: Stemness can also be a 'relational' property that relies on the interaction between entities.
evidence: This is a definitional claim based on metaphysical analysis.

claim: A relational property is not hardwired in a predetermined pool of cells.
source: Unlike the dispositional property, a relational property is not hardwired in a predetermined pool of cells, such as germline stem cells (which give rise to egg and sperm cells).
evidence: This is a definitional distinction between property types.

claim: Germline stem cells give rise to egg and sperm cells.
source: Unlike the dispositional property, a relational property is not hardwired in a predetermined pool of cells, such as germline stem cells (which give rise to egg and sperm cells).
evidence: This is established biological knowledge.

claim: When germline stem cells are removed in fruit flies and mice, they are replaced by differentiated cells that migrate back to the stem cell niche and reacquire stemness.
source: When these stem cells are removed in fruit flies and mice, they are replaced by differentiated cells that migrate back to the stem cell niche, where they reacquire stemness (e.g. Brawley and Matunis, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brawley and Matunis, 2004.

claim: In a mouse model of colon cancer, after cancer stem cells were eliminated, some remaining cancer cells regained stemness in the primary tumor but not in liver metastases.
source: Stemness could also be a relational property in some cancers: recent research in a mouse model of colon cancer has revealed that after cancer stem cells had been eliminated, some remaining cancer cells regained stemness in the primary tumor but not in liver metastases, suggesting that a specific niche is required for the acquisition of stemness (de Sousa e Melo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Sousa e Melo et al., 2017.

claim: The differential regaining of stemness in primary tumor versus liver metastases suggests that a specific niche is required for the acquisition of stemness.
source: Stemness could also be a relational property in some cancers: recent research in a mouse model of colon cancer has revealed that after cancer stem cells had been eliminated, some remaining cancer cells regained stemness in the primary tumor but not in liver metastases, suggesting that a specific niche is required for the acquisition of stemness (de Sousa e Melo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation.

claim: Stemness can be a systemic property, defined as an extrinsic characteristic that is provided and maintained by the system.
source: Finally, stemness can be a 'systemic' property, defined as an extrinsic characteristic that is provided and maintained by the system.
evidence: This is a definitional claim based on metaphysical analysis.

claim: Stemness is a systemic property when non-stem cells acquire stemness features in the absence of a specific environment.
source: Likewise, stemness is a systemic property when non-stem cells acquire stemness features in the absence of a specific environment, which may be the case in cancer.
evidence: This is a definitional claim with speculation about cancer.

claim: Some differentiated cells from breast cancer cell lines can become cancer stem cells again when cultured in vitro.
source: For example, some differentiated cells from breast cancer cell lines can become cancer stem cells again when cultured in vitro (Gupta et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gupta et al., 2011.

claim: The ability of differentiated breast cancer cells to become cancer stem cells in vitro suggests that stemness can be reacquired without a specific niche, with regulation at the system level.
source: This suggests that stemness can be reacquired without a specific niche, with regulation taking place at the system level – here, the cancer cell population.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vitro observation.

claim: Stemness encompasses distinct properties depending on the tissue and context.
source: Stemness therefore encompasses distinct properties, depending on the tissue and context.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of different stemness types.

claim: Which category a stem cell population belongs to depends on whether stemness can be acquired by non-stem cells and whether the niche is mandatory for acquisition or expression of stemness.
source: Which category a stem cell population belongs to depends on two questions that can be addressed experimentally: first, can stemness be acquired by non-stem cells of that tissue? And second, is the niche mandatory for the acquisition of stemness, the expression of stemness, or both?
evidence: This is a logical framework proposed by the authors for classification.

claim: The cancer stem cell model presupposes that cancers maintain an organization similar to that of healthy tissues, with a pool of malignant stem cells acting as the main reservoir for the production of every other cell of the tumor.
source: In oncology, the cancer stem cell model presupposes that cancers maintain an organization similar to that of healthy tissues, with a pool of malignant stem cells acting as the main reservoir for the production of every other cell of the tumor.
evidence: This describes the theoretical framework of the cancer stem cell model.

claim: Cancer stem cells may be generated by the transformation of typical stem cells in the tissue of origin.
source: These cells may be generated by the transformation of typical stem cells in the tissue of origin.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about cancer stem cell origin.

claim: The relationship between the rate of stem cell division and the risk of malignant transformation in a given tissue has led to much controversy in recent years.
source: The relationship between the rate of stem cell division and the risk of malignant transformation in a given tissue has led to much controversy in recent years (Tomasetti et al., 2017; Tomasetti and Vogelstein, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tomasetti et al., 2017 and Tomasetti and Vogelstein, 2015.

claim: Cancer stem cells may emerge from non-stem cells endowed with stemness abilities thanks to genetic and epigenetic alterations.
source: Alternatively, cancer stem cells may emerge from non-stem cells endowed with stemness abilities thanks to genetic and epigenetic alterations.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about an alternative origin of cancer stem cells.

claim: In myeloproliferative neoplasms, hematopoietic cells harboring the JAK2 V617F mutation secrete a molecule that damages the hematopoietic niche.
source: For instance, in some blood cancers known as myeloproliferative neoplasms, hematopoietic cells harboring the JAK2 V617F mutation (which can be found in the majority of patients) secrete a molecule that damages the hematopoietic niche (Arranz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arranz et al., 2014.

claim: The JAK2 V617F mutation can be found in the majority of patients with myeloproliferative neoplasms.
source: For instance, in some blood cancers known as myeloproliferative neoplasms, hematopoietic cells harboring the JAK2 V617F mutation (which can be found in the majority of patients) secrete a molecule that damages the hematopoietic niche (Arranz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the prevalence of this mutation.

claim: Only healthy, but not malignant stem cells, are affected by the degradation of the hematopoietic niche in myeloproliferative neoplasms.
source: Only healthy, but not malignant stem cells, are affected by the degradation of their environment, which suggests that upon transformation into leukemic stem cells, normal stem cells become independent to the niche.
evidence: This is an observation that leads to an inference about niche independence.

claim: Upon transformation into leukemic stem cells, normal stem cells become independent of the niche.
source: Only healthy, but not malignant stem cells, are affected by the degradation of their environment, which suggests that upon transformation into leukemic stem cells, normal stem cells become independent to the niche.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effect of niche degradation.

claim: Transformation of normal hematopoietic stem cells into leukemic stem cells moves stemness from a dispositional property to a categorical property.
source: This moves stemness from a dispositional property in healthy hematopoietic stem cells to a categorical property in leukemic stem cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the change in niche dependence.

claim: The JAK2 V617F mutation contributes to shifting stemness from a dispositional to a categorical property by disrupting the regulation of hematopoietic stem cells by their environment.
source: The JAK2 V617F mutation also contributes to shifting stemness from a dispositional to a categorical property by disrupting the regulation of hematopoietic stem cells by their environment (e.g., Staerk and Constantinescu, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Staerk and Constantinescu, 2012.

claim: In myeloid malignancies, oncogenic events such as KRAS mutations can lead to dysregulations similar to those caused by JAK2 V617F.
source: In other myeloid malignancies, oncogenic events such as KRAS mutations can lead to similar dysregulations.
evidence: This is presented as knowledge about oncogenic mutations in myeloid malignancies.

claim: KRAS mutations can occur either very early in leukemic transformation or later during disease progression.
source: These mutations can occur either very early in leukemic transformation, or later during disease progression (Deininger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Deininger et al., 2017.

claim: Stemness transitioning from a dispositional to a categorical property could happen during the clonal evolution of the disease.
source: This suggests that stemness transitioning from a dispositional to a categorical property could also happen during the clonal evolution of the disease.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of mutations.

claim: In mouse models of squamous cell carcinoma, cells gain migratory and invasive properties through epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.
source: In mouse models of squamous cell carcinoma, a type of skin cancer, cells gain migratory and invasive properties through a mechanism known as a epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.
evidence: This is presented as an observation from mouse models.

claim: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in squamous cell carcinoma can occur either frequently or rarely, depending on the chromatin state of the cell of origin.
source: This process can occur either frequently or rarely, depending on the chromatin state of the cell of origin (Latil et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Latil et al., 2017.

claim: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition can result in stemness acquisition.
source: As this transition can result in stemness acquisition, squamous cell carcinomas may fall into two categories.
evidence: This is presented as an established relationship between the transition and stemness.

claim: In squamous cell carcinomas without frequent epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions, stemness is best described as a dispositional property.
source: In the absence of transition, stemness would best described as a dispositional property: intrinsic to the cells, but only revealed in the right context.
evidence: This is an inference about the type of stemness property based on transition frequency.

claim: In squamous cell carcinomas with frequent epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions, stemness would become a relational property.
source: However, in the presence of frequent transitions, stemness would become a relational property – extrinsic and conditional on epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions.
evidence: This is an inference about the type of stemness property based on transition frequency.

claim: Cancer occurrence and progression could be associated with changes in the nature of stemness.
source: Taken together, cancer occurrence and progression could be associated with changes in the nature of stemness.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the examples presented.

claim: It remains to be seen whether changes in stemness are a consequence of disease progression or one of its requirements.
source: It remains to be seen whether these changes are a consequence of disease progression or one of its requirements.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about an unresolved question.

claim: Current cancer treatment approaches target either malignant cells or surrounding cells.
source: Current treatment approaches target either malignant cells (with chemotherapy, ionizing radiations and targeted therapies), or surrounding cells (with immunotherapy or anti-angiogenic therapies).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer treatment strategies.

claim: If cancer treatments fail to eliminate all cancer stem cells, a relapse may occur.
source: If these treatments fail to eliminate all the cancer stem cells, a relapse may occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cancer stem cell model.

claim: Targeting cancer stem cells depends on the assumption that stemness is an intrinsic property (categorical or dispositional).
source: Targeting cancer stem cells depends on the assumption that stemness is an intrinsic property (i.e., categorical or dispositional); otherwise, the malignant cells would regenerate new cancer stem cells after their elimination.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the presuppositions of a therapeutic strategy.

claim: If stemness is not an intrinsic property, malignant cells would regenerate new cancer stem cells after their elimination.
source: Targeting cancer stem cells depends on the assumption that stemness is an intrinsic property (i.e., categorical or dispositional); otherwise, the malignant cells would regenerate new cancer stem cells after their elimination.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would happen if stemness is not intrinsic.

claim: Niche-targeting relies on the notion that stemness is a niche-dependent property (dispositional or relational).
source: Niche-targeting relies on the notion that stemness is a niche-dependent property (i.e., dispositional or relational).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the presuppositions of a therapeutic strategy.

claim: Changes in the nature of stemness may require therapeutic adaptation.
source: Changes in the nature of stemness may require therapeutic adaptation.
evidence: This is a speculative recommendation based on the analysis.

claim: It would be useful to monitor the impact of genetic and epigenetic alterations on the nature of stemness during disease evolution.
source: It would thus be useful to monitor the impact of genetic and epigenetic alterations on the nature of stemness during the evolution of the disease.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the analysis.

claim: If changes in stemness are driving progression rather than resulting from it, therapeutic interventions that modulate stemness could be beneficial.
source: If changes in stemness are driving progression rather than resulting from it, therapeutic interventions that modulate stemness could also be beneficial.
evidence: This is a speculative recommendation conditional on the causal role of stemness changes.

claim: Stem cell biology is full of conceptual debates.
source: Stem cell biology is full of conceptual debates, and philosophers have contributed to these debates on a range of topics (reviewed in Fagan, 2013b), including the definition of stem cells and the entity/state debate (Fagan, 2013a; Laplane, 2016; Wilson et al., 2007; Leychkis et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to philosophical literature on stem cells.

claim: Philosophers have contributed to debates in stem cell biology on topics including the definition of stem cells and the entity/state debate.
source: Stem cell biology is full of conceptual debates, and philosophers have contributed to these debates on a range of topics (reviewed in Fagan, 2013b), including the definition of stem cells and the entity/state debate (Fagan, 2013a; Laplane, 2016; Wilson et al., 2007; Leychkis et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to philosophical work.

claim: Traditional tools of philosophy, such as the metaphysics of properties, can be applied to stem cell biology to shed light on the fundamental nature of stem cells.
source: Focusing on the nature of stemness, we show how traditional tools of philosophy, such as the metaphysics of properties, can be applied to stem cell biology to shed light on the fundamental nature of stem cells.
evidence: This is a claim about the utility of philosophical methods demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: The proposed classification of stemness draws practical consequences in guiding the choice of an anticancer treatment.
source: More than a simple descriptive characterization, the proposed classification draws practical consequences in guiding the choice of an anticancer treatment.
evidence: This is a claim about the practical utility of the classification presented.

claim: Mammals and insects have distinct types of eyes that have emerged independently throughout evolution as two different but effective solutions to a similar challenge.
source: For instance, mammals and insects have distinct types of eyes that have emerged independently throughout evolution as two different but effective solutions to a similar challenge.
evidence: This is established knowledge from evolutionary biology used as an analogy.

claim: A phylogenetic analysis of stemness could highlight whether different types of stem cells occurred separately during evolution as different solutions to the challenges of tissue maintenance and repair.
source: Similarly, a phylogenetic analysis of stemness could highlight whether the different types of stem cells occurred separately during evolution, as different solutions to the challenges of tissue maintenance and repair.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for future research.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis could deepen the metaphysics of stem cells by identifying whether the four stemness properties depict entities that are biologically independent.
source: In turn, this would deepen the metaphysics of stem cells by identifying whether our four stemness properties depict entities that are biologically independent .
evidence: This is a speculative claim about how phylogenetic analysis could inform metaphysical understanding.

claim: It is only by bridging disciplines such as experimental biology, medicine, phylogeny and philosophy that stem cells will be properly understood.
source: It is only by bridging disciplines such as experimental biology, medicine, phylogeny and philosophy that stem cells will be properly understood.
evidence: This is a normative claim about the interdisciplinary approach needed for understanding stem cells.
